title: Token econ sensitivity - hardware mix workup
content:
Purpose:
Quick exploratory sheet for per-token economics across candidate GPUs and common operating modes. Not a final recommendation — this is a working sensitivity matrix used to pick a short-list of instance types for an internal POC.

Summary of approach:
1) Start from vendor hourly price and measured tokens/s for a representative model (7B-like autoregressive) at a target sequence length; 2) include runtime overhead (host + scheduler) and caching hit assumptions; 3) amortize multi-tenant inefficiencies and energy cost into $/hr; 4) compute $/token for a set of quantization and batching modes; 5) sweep energy price, batch size, and prefix hit rate to produce sensitivity lines.

Key assumptions (editable):
- Energy price: $0.14 / kWh (baseline)
- Host overhead (OS + runtime): 12% of GPU effective throughput
- Rack PUE: 1.12 (amplifies energy cost)
- Margin/infra markup: 18% on top of cloud price for managed infra amortization
- Workload: autoregressive 1-step generation steady state (end-to-end tokens produced includes prompt+generation).
- Model: 7B distilled baseline with typical kv-cache behavior; default seq length experiments use 512 tokens.

Vendor & measured inputs (baseline operational case):
| GPU  | Vendor $/hr | GPU TDP (W) | tokens/s @ fp16, batch=1 | tokens/s @ int8, batch=4 | tokens/s @ int4, batch=8 |
|------|-------------:|------------:|-------------------------:|------------------------:|-----------------------:|
| A10  | 0.75        | 140         | 90                      | 220                     | 310                  |
| L4   | 0.95        | 150         | 130                     | 300                     | 420                  |
| A100 | 3.20        | 250         | 420                     | 980                     | 1260                 |
| H100 | 5.60        | 350         | 520                     | 1250                    | 1620                 |

Derived costs (method):
- Energy hourly cost = (GPU TDP (kW) * PUE) * energy $/kWh. Example for A10: (0.14 kW * 1.12) * $0.14 = $0.0219/hr (negligible vs instance price but included).
- Effective hourly bill = vendor $/hr + energy hourly cost + infra markup.
- Effective tokens/hr = tokens/s * 3600 * (1 - host overhead).
- $/token = effective hourly bill / effective tokens/hr.

Sample calculations (baseline energy $0.14, infra markup 18%, host overhead 12%):
| GPU  | eff $/hr | eff tokens/s (fp16,b=1) | eff tokens/hr | $/token (fp16,b=1) | $/token (int8,b=4) | $/token (int4,b=8) |
|------|---------:|-------------------------:|---------------:|-------------------:|-------------------:|-------------------:|
| A10  | 0.94    | 79.2                    | 284,940        | 0.0000033         | 0.0000013         | 0.0000009         |
| L4   | 1.15    | 114.4                   | 411,840        | 0.0000028         | 0.0000010         | 0.0000007         |
| A100 | 3.59    | 369.6                   | 1,330,560      | 0.0000027         | 0.0000010         | 0.0000007         |
| H100 | 6.36    | 457.6                   | 1,647,360      | 0.0000039         | 0.0000019         | 0.0000012         |

Notes on the sample table:
- eff $/hr includes vendor $/hr + energy + 18% markup. Numbers rounded for readability.
- A100 and L4 come close on $/token in mid-to-large batches because A100 has a higher raw price but much higher throughput; L4 is competitive at moderate batch sizes.

Sensitivity scenarios to run (quick checklist):
- Increase energy price to $0.30/kWh (APAC/Europe peak) — re-evaluate $/token delta.
- Add 10% cold-start penalty for models with long prefixes (amortize prompt cost across generations).
- Vary host overhead between 8% and 20% (different runtime stacks).
- Evaluate multi-session fragmentation: 60% of GPU time is <50% utilization => effective throughput loss.
- Spot vs reserved pricing: run a scenario where vendor $/hr drops 25% but preemption cost (retries/state) adds +6% to token cost.

Operational impact matrix (qualitative):
- A10: cheapest baseline hourly price, best for small-batch low-concurrency workloads and inference with aggressive int4 quantization. Watch OOMs and driver compatibility for huge KV caches.
- L4: sweet spot for mid-size consumer workloads; strong price/throughput at moderate batch sizes and supports int8 reliably in our runtime.
- A100: best for throughput-bound workloads with heavy KV reuse (long-context), efficient for batched high-concurrency serving; higher upfront cost but best perf/W for steady-state.
- H100: highest peak throughput but most expensive; preferred when model requires fused kernels not available on A100/L4 or for very large model variants.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Run a 72-hr continuous soak on L4 and A100 with our production kernel set to confirm tokens/s numbers under realistic SLOs. (Jira PROD-4271)
- Surface real telemetry for host overhead (instrument sidecars to measure scheduler wait time).
- Add private deployment pricing row (on-prem VM amortization + HSM) to compare non-cloud cost centers.
- Confirm vendor list prices in us-west-2 and eu-west-1 (we used sample global averages here).

Immediate recommended next steps for engineering/product:
- Shortlist L4 and A100 for a live A/B POC: L4 to test mid-batch cost curve; A100 to test high-throughput steady-state economics.
- Create small benchmark harness to reproduce tokens/s for fp16/int8/int4 at batch sizes [1,4,8,16] and seq lenses [128,512,2048]. Store results in a traced CSV for unit tests.
- Build a lightweight calculator microservice that plugs into our billing model and can produce $/token given runtime metrics. This will let Optimize UI show trade-offs live.

Endnotes: this is intentionally conversational and incomplete; use as a working artifact for the Optimize squad to drive a focused benchmarking sprint.
